text: Initial cross-check: the assigned Q is Aero Hand Open, a tendon-driven robotic hand and simulation-to-real PPO system (Q lines 125-137, 643-645). P is a quadratic resource-allocation/CVaR mechanism note whose “Q” means Garjani et al., not this assigned Q (P lines 13-17, 48-53). Thus P’s propositions do not directly apply to the hand; I will test whether its fixed-batch tail-risk/participation argument yields a genuine controller-evaluation or deployment result, and avoid importing the mechanism claims as if they were about robotics.

The supplied pair is topically mismatched: Q is Aero Hand Open (tendon-driven hand, identified actuation map, sim-to-real PPO); P is a fixed-batch CVaR / quadratic allocation-mechanism note. P Sec. 1 calls Garjani et al. its Q and Wang et al. its P, but those are not the supplied Q/P. I will analyze the actual attached pair, testing whether P\(\mathrm{CVaR}\) value-error reasoning can certify tail risk for Q\(\mathrm{Aero}\) transfer. Q Sec. Results reports open-loop replay and no logged physical cube pose; this is likely a measurement obstacle.

I am sharpening the question from strategic participation to a closed-loop tail-risk transfer certificate for Q. For a fixed policy \(\pi\), define paired full-episode losses \(L^{\rm real}_{\pi}\) and \(L^{\rm sim}_{\pi}\), and residual \(D_{\pi}=L^{\rm real}_{\pi}-L^{\rm sim}_{\pi}\). CVaR subadditivity gives \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta}(L^{\rm real}_{\pi})\leq \operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta}(L^{\rm sim}_{\pi})+\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta}(D_{\pi})\). P Sec. Conditional value-level guarantees supplies a finite-batch value-error template for estimating the terms. Q Sec. Separating transmission mismatch from policy feedback already motivates paired replay, but its replay is open-loop and Q Sec. Zero-shot deployment says physical cube pose is not logged, so present data cannot score closed-loop episode losses. I will test whether this is a useful conditional advance or merely generic CVaR algebra.

Sharpened question (changed from whether P’s mechanism theorem transfers): can finite-batch CVaR of episode-level cube loss justify a tail-risk claim for Aero Hand Open? Q defines mean-style PPO reward with rotation/fall terms (Q lines 673-688), trains with 8192 parallel simulator environments (Q lines 741-745), but reports a nominal 15 s simulation rollout (Q lines 760-764) and hardware rotation without logged cube pose (Q lines 773-784). P’s (e_n=L_n\delta_n+U_n\sqrt{2\pi}/(\beta_n\sqrt{s_n})) is a bound for expected empirical CVaR at valid queries, not a realised-batch or sim-to-hardware guarantee (P lines 56-64). Thus the formal premise needed to certify Q’s hardware tail risk is absent. Q also says cube friction and mass randomisation draws were overwritten (Q lines 690-694), and identifies large thumb excursion mismatch (Q lines 590-599); those are concrete transfer axes to test, not quantified episode-loss distribution shifts.

Prior-work check weakens novelty of my entry #3. Vincent, Feldman, Schwager, \(\textit{Guarantees on Robot System Performance Using Stochastic Simulation Rollouts}\), IEEE T-RO 2024, https://doi.org/10.1109/TRO.2024.3444070, already gives finite-sample CVaR bounds for open/closed-loop robot policies, distribution-shift robustness, and multiple-policy correction (including Shadow Hand). SureSim, https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04354, uses paired real/sim robot evaluations for finite-sample mean-performance inference. Thus a generic CVaR certificate or paired residual design is not itself a publication novelty. Search queries: CVaR sim-to-real transfer bound model error trajectory risk reinforcement learning arxiv; CVaR policy evaluation simulator real residual confidence bound paired samples; sim2real CVaR risk discrepancy robot policy evaluation certification. I am checking whether Q-specific thumb/feedback measurements yield a narrower falsifiable experiment, while treating existing P propositions as unrelated to Q hardware.

A task-level calculation isolates the gap. Let episode fall loss be (F\in\{0,1\}), (p=\Pr(F=1)), and upper-tail mass (\beta). Then (\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta}(F)=\min\{1,p/\beta\}). For a one-episode empirical CVaR, (\mathbb E\widehat{\operatorname{CVaR}}_{\beta}(F)=p); e.g. (p=0.02,\beta=0.05) gives true risk (0.4) versus expected surrogate (0.02). A safe candidate with constant loss (0.1) reverses their ordering. This is the controller-selection analogue of P’s one-sample surrogate mismatch (P lines 36-48), but Q does not select policies by CVaR, so it is a prospective test, not a defect proved in Q. For hardware validation, even zero falls in (m) independent episodes gives a one-sided (95\%\) binomial bound (p\leq1-0.05^{1/m}); certifying (\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.05}(F)\leq0.1) this way requires (m\geq598). Q reports no such repeated hardware episode count or logged cube pose (Q lines 773-784). The iid and loss-definition assumptions are essential.

Correction to #6: shell quoting stripped the TeX delimiters. Let episode fall loss be \(F\in\{0,1\}\), \(p=\Pr(F=1)\), and upper-tail mass \(\beta\). Then \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta}(F)=\min\{1,p/\beta\}\). For one episode, \(\mathbb E\widehat{\operatorname{CVaR}}_{\beta}(F)=p\); for \(p=0.02,\beta=0.05\), these are \(0.02\) versus \(0.4\). A constant-loss candidate at \(0.1\) reverses the ordering. With \(m\) independent zero-fall hardware trials, the exact one-sided \(95\%\) binomial upper bound is \(p\leq1-0.05^{1/m}\), so \(m\geq598\) is needed to certify \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{0.05}(F)\leq0.1\) by this route. This is a prospective risk-evaluation calculation, not a claim that Q optimizes CVaR.

Best pair-specific line I find is an experiment, not an established theorem: compare the tail of closed-loop cube-rotation loss before/after a thumb-model correction and with cube friction/mass varied. Q Secs. Kinematic/Dynamic validation says thumb cable excursions miss by \(32.7\%\) and \(31.2\%\), the remaining flexor-radius error survives software mapping, and simulated rise time is \(10\) to \(40\,\mathrm{ms}\) faster (Q lines 590-625). Q Sec. Domain randomisation says cube friction/mass draws are overwritten (Q lines 690-694). Q Sec. Results says only an open-loop command replay was paired, and physical cube pose was not logged (Q lines 773-802). These measurements cannot bound closed-loop loss: equal motor traces need not imply equal contact outcome when cube state/friction is hidden. P Sec. Conditional value-level guarantees (lines 56-84) bounds expected empirical CVaR under same-distribution bounded losses and a valid oracle, not a realised batch or sim-to-real shift. A defensible experiment would log cube pose/falls, use paired initial conditions and independent complete episodes, estimate CVaR with finite-sample/multiple-comparison correction, and measure whether thumb correction changes the lower-tail rotation/fall outcomes. No such episode-level data are in Q; no publication result follows from the current pair alone.

Cross-check of ada #7: the Bernoulli formula and \(m\geq598\) zero-fall calculation are correct: \(\operatorname{CVaR}_{\beta}(F)=\min\{1,p/\beta\}\) and \(1-0.05^{1/m}\leq0.005\) first holds at \(m=598\). It is a sharp illustration of the episode count needed for a \(\beta=0.05\) claim. It cannot establish a failure of Q, which optimizes PPO reward rather than empirical CVaR, and Q supplies neither a constant-loss comparison policy nor repeated hardware fall data. The formal robot-CVaR evaluation problem, distribution shift, and multiple-policy correction also appear in Vincent et al. 2024 (https://doi.org/10.1109/TRO.2024.3444070); novelty would have to come from a new thumb/contact experiment or a demonstrably tighter special-purpose bound.

Correction to #4: the intended TeX is \(e_n=L_n\delta_n+U_n\sqrt{2\pi}/(\beta_n\sqrt{s_n})\). Cross-check of emmy #5 confirms that Vincent, Feldman and Schwager already give finite-sample CVaR bounds for arbitrary robot policies, explicit distribution-shift treatment, and multiple-policy correction on a Shadow Hand (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10874). SureSim gives paired real/simulation mean-performance inference (https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.04354). I searched “site:arxiv.org CVaR domain randomization sim-to-real reinforcement learning robotics”, “site:proceedings.mlr.press CVaR sim-to-real reinforcement learning robot risk”, and “site:arxiv.org dexterous manipulation CVaR tail risk contact uncertainty”. The binary-loss calculation #7 diagnoses the missing evidence in Q but is not a novel certification method.

My current judgement: no supported publication result follows from the supplied pair alone. The strongest falsifiable next study is whether Q’s measured thumb transmission mismatch, simulator response-time lead, and absent cube friction/mass randomisation cause worse closed-loop tail outcomes for cube rotation (Q lines 590-625, 690-694, 773-802). A clean comparison must define full-episode loss and log physical cube pose/falls; distinguish correcting the simulator followed by retraining from changing the deployed mapping, since each changes a different part of the loop; and use independent test episodes with predeclared tail mass and correction for policy selection. P’s one-sample bias and expected-surrogate bound (P lines 36-75) motivate caution about finite-batch tail scores, but neither proves this hand fails nor handles simulator-to-hardware shift. Existing robot-policy CVaR guarantees at https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10874 make a generic certificate insufficient as novelty. Without outcome data, my binary-loss example is a diagnostic counterexample, not the sought advance.

Cross-check of ada #12 against Q Sec. Zero-shot deployment: Q lines 786-791 says commissioning opened cable scales by \(20\%\) to \(30\%\) and closed nominal pose by \(4\) to \(8\,\mathrm{mm}\); Q lines 773-784 says physical cube pose was not logged. Therefore a comparison of thumb-model correction and tail loss must record or fix those deployment settings and distinguish simulation correction with retraining from deployment-map correction at a fixed policy. The existing open-loop action replay (Q lines 798-802) observes actuator response under shared commands, not the closed-loop cube-loss distribution. P lines 56-64 bounds expected empirical CVaR for bounded same-distribution losses; it supplies no outcome or shift bound for this comparison. This strengthens the experimental specification, but the pair still contains no publication-ready causal result.

Cross-check of emmy #14 and Q lines 649-660, 722-738, 773-802: the deployed network is unchanged, but finger action scales and nominal pose are retuned, and deployment removes training observation noise. Q evaluates its nominal simulator rollout under deployment settings (lines 760-764). The open-loop replay compares actuator channels, while cube pose is unlogged on hardware; hence agreement of those channels cannot by itself attribute a task-level rotation or fall gap to policy feedback. Contact dynamics may differ even when actuator traces agree. For a causal tail-risk experiment, fix the deployment settings across arms, log cube pose and falls, compare complete closed-loop episodes under matched initial states, and predeclare whether the intervention is simulator correction plus retraining or deployed-map correction at a fixed policy. P lines 56-64 controls an expected empirical CVaR surrogate within one distribution, so it does not close this identification gap.
